decision.explanation: Let u=2x-3, so du=2 dx. Then the integral is 3∫u^{-4} du=-u^{-3}+C=-1/(2x-3)^3+C.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int 6(2x-3)^{-4}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=2x-3.$Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6(2x-3)^{-4}\,\text{d}x & =\int 6{u}^{-4}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\int {u}^{-4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}){u}^{-3}+C \\  & =-{u}^{-3}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{(2x-3)^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-\frac{1}{(2x-3)^{3}}+C] & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-\frac{1}{(2x-3)^{3}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(2x-3)^{-3}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =-(-3)\cdot (2x-3)^{-4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x-3)+0 \\  & =3\cdot (2x-3)^{-4}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{6}{(2x-3)^{4}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Integrating an Algebraic Function With Negative Integer Exponent
content.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int 6(2x-3)^{-4}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=2x-3.$Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6(2x-3)^{-4}\,\text{d}x & =\int 6{u}^{-4}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\int {u}^{-4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}){u}^{-3}+C \\  & =-{u}^{-3}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{(2x-3)^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-\frac{1}{(2x-3)^{3}}+C] & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-\frac{1}{(2x-3)^{3}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(2x-3)^{-3}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =-(-3)\cdot (2x-3)^{-4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x-3)+0 \\  & =3\cdot (2x-3)^{-4}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{6}{(2x-3)^{4}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Rewrite the integrand as (y+11)^(5/3). The power rule gives (3/8)(y+11)^(8/3)+C, which equals (3/8)∛((y+11)^8)+C.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (y+11)^{5/3}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Now, we let $u=y+11.$ Then differentiating with respect to $y$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}y=\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $u$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (y+11)^{5/3}\,\text{d}y & =\int {u}^{5/3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{8/3}}{8/3}+C \\  & =\frac{3}{8}(y+11)^{8/3}+C \\  & =\frac{3}{8}\sqrt[3]{(y+11)^{8}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[\frac{3}{8}\sqrt[3]{(y+11)^{8}}] & =\frac{3}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[\sqrt[3]{(y+11)^{8}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(C) \\  & =\frac{3}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[(y+11)^{8/3}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(C) \\  & =\frac{3}{8}\cdot \frac{8}{3}(y+11)^{5/3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y+11)+0 \\  & =(y+11)^{5/3}\cdot 1 \\  & =\sqrt[3]{(y+11)^{5}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3

Calculate the integral ∫(y+11)53dy.

a
38(y+11)83+C
b
(y+11)83+C
c
8(y+11)53+C
d
3(y+11)83+C
e
83(y+11)23+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we rewrite the integral as

∫(y+11)5/3dy.

Now, we let u=y+11. Then differentiating with respect to y gives dudy=1⟹dy=du.

We now write our integral in terms of u, calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of u at the very end:

∫(y+11)5/3dy=∫u5/3du=u8/38/3+C=38(y+11)8/3+C=38(y+11)83+C

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

ddy[38(y+11)83]=38⋅ddy[(y+11)83]+ddy(C)=38⋅ddy[(y+11)8/3]+ddy(C)=38⋅83(y+11)5/3⋅ddy(y+11)+0=(y+11)5/3⋅1=(y+11)53✓

content.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (y+11)^{5/3}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Now, we let $u=y+11.$ Then differentiating with respect to $y$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}y=\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $u$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (y+11)^{5/3}\,\text{d}y & =\int {u}^{5/3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{8/3}}{8/3}+C \\  & =\frac{3}{8}(y+11)^{8/3}+C \\  & =\frac{3}{8}\sqrt[3]{(y+11)^{8}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[\frac{3}{8}\sqrt[3]{(y+11)^{8}}] & =\frac{3}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[\sqrt[3]{(y+11)^{8}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(C) \\  & =\frac{3}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[(y+11)^{8/3}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(C) \\  & =\frac{3}{8}\cdot \frac{8}{3}(y+11)^{5/3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y+11)+0 \\  & =(y+11)^{5/3}\cdot 1 \\  & =\sqrt[3]{(y+11)^{5}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int {(s+1)}^{-3/5}\,\text{d}s.
$$

Now, we let  $u=s+1.$ Then differentiating with respect to $s$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}s}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}s=\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $u$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(s+1)}^{-3/5}\,\text{d}s & =\int {u}^{-3/5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2/5}{u}^{2/5}+C \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{u}^{2/5}+C \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{(s+1)}^{2/5}+C \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\sqrt[5]{{(s+1)}^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}[\frac{5}{2}\sqrt[5]{{(s+1)}^{2}}+C] & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}[\sqrt[5]{{(s+1)}^{2}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(C) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}[{(s+1)}^{2/5}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(C) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{5}{(s+1)}^{-3/5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(s+1)+0 \\  & ={(s+1)}^{-3/5}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt[5]{{(s+1)}^{3}}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int -15(5x-7)^{-4}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=5x-7.$Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -15(5x-7)^{-4}\,\text{d}x & =\int -15{u}^{-4}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-3\int {u}^{-4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-3\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}){u}^{-3}+C \\  & ={u}^{-3}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{(5x-7)^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{(5x-7)^{3}}+C] & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{(5x-7)^{3}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(5x-7)^{-3}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =-3\cdot (5x-7)^{-4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5x-7)+0 \\  & =-3\cdot (5x-7)^{-4}\cdot 5 \\  & =-\frac{15}{(5x-7)^{4}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
